items.excerpt: ## Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Iran's government says seven oil tankers have caught fire or been damaged in the strategic Strait of Hormuz. This comes amid rising tensions over the prospect of a return to all-out war. Iranian state television cites the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy which threatens to strike U.S. military bases if the United States continues guiding commercial ships through the strait. The U.S. is meanwhile sending more military assets to the region. Mediators are trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to talks. Iran has proposed ending the conflict if the U.S. meets certain conditions. But U.S. President Donald Trump rejected it although discussions have continued. ## Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia has launched a nighttime missile barrage on Kyiv while its military says it intercepted more than 800 Ukrainian drones targeting Moscow and other Russian cities. The attacks dampen hopes for peace talks. Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed “in principle” to resume negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S. but no date is set. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday reported deadly attacks across 12 regions with Kyiv enduring significant damage. Ukraine is bracing for winter as Russia targets its power grid. A U.S. envoy faced criticism for flattering Putin which highlights ongoing tensions and challenges in reaching a resolution. ## Iran says 7 tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, and other Mideast news Iran's state television reports that seven oil tankers have been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. This happened overnight Thursday, possibly marking the largest single-day incident since the Iran war began on February 28. Four tankers caught fire after being targeted, while three others were immobilized by naval mines. The report warns that the Revolutionary Guard may target U.S. bases if the U.S. tries to allow tankers to transit through other parts of the strait. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Defense Ministry warns that Houthi rallies could be targeted, and Saudi Arabia reports two deaths from an attack on King Fahd International Airport. ## Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a new report finds WASHINGTON (AP) — A new report shows President Donald Trump's administration has sharply increased deportations over the past year. A report released Thursday by the Migration Policy Institute shows deportations are on track to reach 660,000 since last October. That's a 26% increase from President Joe Biden's administration but below the 1.86 million deportations recorded in 2000, under President Bill Clinton. Trump's administration has pushed through restrictions on both legal and illegal immigration. Voluntary departures are at an all-time high, with 170,000 immigrants choosing to leave the United States since Trump returned to office. Trump's administration no longer regularly releases immigration data, making it difficult to gauge its progress. The Republican administration says it's transparent. ## Violent Arizona storms bring possible tornado, toppled trees and golf ball-size hail PHOENIX (AP) — A possible tornado has caused significant damage in a central Arizona community, with trees falling onto homes and utility poles knocked down. items.title: Market sell-off gains steam on Iran war, high AI spending fears
items.excerpt: U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the U.S. would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold on to recent gains. The S&P 500 closed down 1.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.6%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4% to $113 a barrel, its highest level since May, while U.S. crude gained more than 2% to close at more than $99 a barrel. Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the past several weeks — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets amid riskier ones like tech stocks selling off. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell below 5% for the first time since late September.

items.title: 10-year Treasury yield tumbles below 5% to lowest level in nearly a month
items.excerpt: Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist, which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%. ... This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices. Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%. Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude Add To Watchlist futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel. ... Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. ... "The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. items.excerpt: Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese's 'What Happens at Night' Oct 22, 2026 1:12pm PT ... # Charli xcx Joins Martin Scorsese’s ‘What Happens at Night’ With Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence (EXCLUSIVE) By ... Charli xcx and Martin Scorsese‘s collaboration is extending beyond the cover for her new album “Music, Fashion, Film.” Sources tell Variety that the pop star has a cameo in the Oscar-winning director’s upcoming movie “What Happens at Night” alongside Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence. Described as a Gothic psychological horror film, the Apple and StudioCanal production follows an American married couple who travel to a small European town to adopt a baby — but as they struggle to claim their child, the less they seem to know about themselves. Charli’s part in the film is being kept under wraps. She joins a cast that also includes Mads Mikkelsen, Patricia Clarkson and Jared Harris. Representatives for Charli, Apple and StudioCanal did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment. ... The “Brat” singer has been making a name for herself in the film world as of late, appearing in seven movies over the past two years. That includes “The Moment,” a mockumentary directed by her frequent collaborator Aidan Zamiri which cheekily satirized the commercial success she achieved with “Brat.” Cinema even inspired her latest album, “Music, Fashion, Film,” which pictures John Cale, Marc Jacobs and Scorsese on the cover to symbolize each art form. Charli is currently wrapping up her tour for the record in the U.S., with the final show of the leg in Las Vegas on Friday before she heads to Europe in February. “What Happens at Night” marks Scorsese’s follow-up to 2023’s “Killers of the Flower Moon,” which also starred DiCaprio and was nominated for 10 Oscars, including best picture. A release date has not yet been set.

Anderson's death comes on the heels of a celebration of another country icon, Dolly Parton, who was honored with a star-studded tribute ceremony. The Dolly Parton tribute, presented by the CMA, brought together a wide range of stars, including Sabrina Carpenter, Julia Roberts, and Oprah, who all came together to celebrate Parton's legacy as a unifying force in music. The ceremony even featured a special performance by Zac Brown, who delivered an emotional duet with Parton herself. If you missed the tribute, you can still catch it tonight, and we've got details on how to watch for free.
